passages.t: ‘To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “Of David” (verse 1). Then: “To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul; in You, my God, I trust” (verses 1-2). His first fear is shame: “Do not let me be put to shame; do not let my enemies exult over me” (verse 2).

He asks to be taught. “Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths” (verse 4). He asks God to remember some things and forget others: “Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my rebellious acts; remember me according to Your loving devotion” (verse 7). And he asks plainly, “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, forgive my iniquity, for it is great” (verse 11).

Near the end the prayer grows lonely. “Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted” (verse 16). “Consider my affliction and trouble, and take away all my sins” (verse 18).

The last verse widens to the whole people: “Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 25 is an acrostic, an alphabet poem. In Hebrew each verse begins with the next letter of the alphabet, with a gap or two. The last verse stands outside the alphabet, and Psalm 34 ends the same way, with an extra verse that begins with the same letter. Many scholars think verse 22 turned one person's prayer into a prayer for all Israel. An alphabet poem was easy to learn by heart, and it says, in its shape, ‘everything from A to Z’.

Three words come back again and again: ‘shame’, ‘way’ and ‘wait’. In Israel, shame was not just a feeling. It was public. To be ‘put to shame’ was to be seen by everyone to have trusted something that failed you. So ‘do not let me be put to shame’ means: do not let my trust in You turn out to be foolish.

‘Wait’ in the Psalms is not sitting still. It is looking out for God, the way a watchman looks for the morning.
passages.later:
Isaiah promises, “But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:31). Paul says that “hope does not disappoint us” (Romans 5:5), using the same idea as ‘not put to shame’.

The prayer to be taught God's way is answered in Jesus, who said, “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6). James says that anyone who lacks wisdom “should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault” (James 1:5).

The tax collector in Jesus' story prayed with the same honesty as verse 11: “God, have mercy on me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13).
passages.asks:
Verse 7 asks a gentle, searching question. What would you like God to forget? The psalm says you may ask him to, and it says he remembers you ‘according to Your loving devotion’, not according to your past.

If you are lonely, verse 16 gives you words. You do not need to dress loneliness up as something else before you bring it to God.

The psalm also teaches a pattern for any day: lift up your soul (verse 1), ask to be taught (verse 4), confess (verse 11), and pray for others too (verse 22).
